title: What happens to a "zombie" producer after a network partition heals (epoch fencing)?
shortTitle: What happens to a "zombie" producer after a network partition heals (epoch fencing)?

s1_definition.profdef: A zombie producer is a transactional producer instance that was presumed dead and replaced, but which is actually still alive and may try to write again after a network partition heals. Kafka fences zombies using the producer id and a monotonically increasing epoch. When a new producer instance initializes transactions with the same transactional id, the transaction coordinator bumps the epoch, and any write or commit that arrives from the old, lower epoch is rejected with a ProducerFenced error. So when the partition heals, the zombie's late writes are refused and it is forced to shut down, which preserves exactly-once correctness.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India issues a teller a numbered authorization stamp to approve transfers. The teller walks into the vault, the door jams (network partition), and the branch assumes the teller is gone. The branch promotes a replacement and issues a new stamp with a higher number, declaring the old number void. Later the vault door opens and the original teller walks out still carrying the old stamp, trying to approve a transfer from before. The clerk checks the stamp number, sees it is lower than the current valid number, and refuses it on the spot. The old teller is sent home. That stamp-number check is epoch fencing, and it stops the "ghost" teller from double-approving a transfer for Rajesh.
s1_definition.oneliner: The transactional id plus a monotonically increasing epoch fences zombies — when a partition heals, the old producer's lower epoch is rejected with ProducerFenced, so its stale writes and commits never land.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A zombie producer is a transactional producer instance that was presumed dead and replaced, but which is actually still alive and may try to write again after a network partition heals. Kafka fences zombies using the producer id and a monotonically increasing epoch. When a new producer instance initializes transactions with the same transactional id, the transaction coordinator bumps the epoch, and any write or commit that arrives from the old, lower epoch is rejected with a ProducerFenced error. So when the partition heals, the zombie's late writes are refused and it is forced to shut down, which preserves exactly-once correctness.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India issues a teller a numbered authorization stamp to approve transfers. The teller walks into the vault, the door jams (network partition), and the branch assumes the teller is gone. The branch promotes a replacement and issues a new stamp with a higher number, declaring the old number void. Later the vault door opens and the original teller walks out still carrying the old stamp, trying to approve a transfer from before. The clerk checks the stamp number, sees it is lower than the current valid number, and refuses it on the spot. The old teller is sent home. That stamp-number check is epoch fencing, and it stops the "ghost" teller from double-approving a transfer for Rajesh.

**One line to remember:** The transactional id plus a monotonically increasing epoch fences zombies — when a partition heals, the old producer's lower epoch is rejected with ProducerFenced, so its stale writes and commits never land.

sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India settles trades and transfers with a transactional producer so that each settlement either fully commits to the `settlements` topic or not at all. Rajesh (SAV2001) initiates a transfer to Priya (CUR3001) and the settlement must be exactly-once.

Problem 1 — the settlement producer pod loses network connectivity mid-transaction while committing Rajesh's transfer. The orchestrator restarts a fresh pod with the same transactional id to keep settlements flowing. This is exactly the zombie setup: now two instances could both believe they are the settlement producer.

Problem 2 — the original pod's network heals, and it tries to finish committing the same transfer it started. Without protection, this could produce a duplicate settlement, double-crediting Priya. This is exactly what epoch fencing prevents: the new pod bumped the epoch on init, so the old pod's commit arrives with a stale epoch and is rejected.

Our runnable demo models a `TransactionCoordinator` that tracks the current epoch per transactional id, a `TransactionalProducer` that holds the epoch it was given, and a `ZombieScenario` driver. We start producer A at epoch five, simulate a partition, start producer B which bumps to epoch six, then heal the partition and have producer A attempt a commit. The coordinator rejects A with a fencing error, A closes itself, and B proceeds, so Priya is credited exactly once. The classes are `ZombieFencingDemo`, `TransactionCoordinator`, `TransactionalProducer`, and `ProducerFencedException`.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: one transactional id `settlement-tx-1`, a settlement of Rajesh debiting and Priya crediting the same amount, and a network partition that occurs mid-transaction.

Step 1: Producer A calls initTransactions. The coordinator registers `settlement-tx-1`, assigns a producer id, and sets the epoch to five. A begins a transaction to settle the transfer.

Step 2: A network partition isolates A before it can commit. Its transaction is open but unfinished, and consumers with read-committed isolation cannot see any of its records because there is no commit marker.

Step 3: The orchestrator concludes A is dead and starts Producer B with the same transactional id. B calls initTransactions. The coordinator bumps the epoch to six and aborts any in-flight transaction tied to epoch five. B now owns the transactional id at epoch six.

Step 4: B begins its own transaction, writes the debit and credit, and commits at epoch six. Priya is credited exactly once and the records become visible to read-committed consumers.

Step 5: The network heals and zombie A, still holding epoch five, tries to commit. The broker compares epoch five against the current epoch six and rejects the request with ProducerFenced. A's late commit never lands, so there is no duplicate credit. A treats the exception as fatal and closes itself.

Final output:

```
[2026-10-24 22:02:11] [INFO] Producer A initialized with epoch 5
[2026-10-24 22:02:11] [WARNING] Network partition isolates Producer A mid-transaction
[2026-10-24 22:02:11] [INFO] Producer B initialized with epoch 6 (A's epoch now stale)
[2026-10-24 22:02:11] [INFO] COMMIT ok (epoch 6): Priya credited by B (exactly once)
[2026-10-24 22:02:11] [WARNING] Network heals — zombie Producer A attempts to commit
[2026-10-24 22:02:11] [SEVERE] ProducerFenced: A epoch 5 < current 6 — commit REJECTED, no duplicate credit
[2026-10-24 22:02:11] [INFO] Zombie producer closed, epoch 5
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Transactional id: settlement-tx-1
    │
    ▼
  Producer A: initTransactions() -> epoch 5
    │ beginTransaction(), write DEBIT/CREDIT
    ▼
  ╳ NETWORK PARTITION (A isolated, transaction uncommitted, invisible to read_committed)
    │
    ├─ orchestrator starts Producer B
    │     │ initTransactions() -> coordinator bumps epoch to 6, aborts A's in-flight txn
    │     ▼
    │   Producer B: commit at epoch 6 -> Priya credited EXACTLY ONCE (visible)
    │
    ▼ NETWORK HEALS
  Zombie Producer A: commit at epoch 5
    │ broker: incoming epoch 5 != current epoch 6
    ▼
  ProducerFencedException (fatal) -> A.close(), NO duplicate credit
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Transactional Producer and Fencing ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Guard Clause: verifyEpoch() rejects stale-epoch commits          │
  │  Template Method (implicit): begin -> send -> commit/abort flow    │
  │  State Pattern: producer lifecycle INIT -> IN_TXN -> COMMITTED/FENCED│
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: Coordinator owns epochs; Producer owns its send lifecycle     │
  │  O: new fencing policy lives in Coordinator, producer unchanged   │
  │  D: service depends on the producer abstraction, not broker wire  │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │  TransactionalProducer        │───────▶│  TransactionCoordinator       │
  │ ──────────────────────────────│ uses   │ ──────────────────────────────│
  │ - txnId: String               │        │ - epochByTxnId: Map<Str,Int>  │
  │ - epoch: int                  │        │ ──────────────────────────────│
  │ ──────────────────────────────│        │ + registerAndBumpEpoch(txnId) │
  │ + initTransactions()          │        │ + currentEpoch(txnId): int    │
  │ + beginTransaction()          │        │ + verifyEpoch(txnId, epoch)   │
  │ + commitTransaction()         │        │    throws ProducerFenced      │
  │ + close()                     │        └──────────────────────────────┘
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Producer Lifecycle ──────────────────────────────

  [INIT (epoch n)] ──begin──→ [IN_TXN] ──commit (epoch == current)──→ [COMMITTED]
        │                         │
        │ newer instance bumps    │ commit with stale epoch
        │ epoch to n+1            ▼
        └─────────────────→ [FENCED] ──→ close(), fatal, no retry

  ── Call Chain (zombie heal) ───────────────────────────────────────

  1. A.initTransactions() -> epoch 5
  2. A.beginTransaction()    // partition hits here
  3. B.initTransactions() -> coordinator bumps epoch to 6 (A's in-flight aborted)
  4. B.beginTransaction(); B.commitTransaction() -> verifyEpoch(6==6) ok
  5. A.commitTransaction() -> verifyEpoch(5==6?) -> ProducerFencedException
  6. A.close()  // zombie removed, no duplicate settlement
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A zombie producer is a transactional producer instance that everyone assumed was dead and replaced, but which is actually still alive and might try to write again once a network partition heals. Kafka handles this with the transactional id combined with a monotonically increasing epoch. You give a producer role a stable transactional id, and every time a producer initializes transactions under that id, the transaction coordinator bumps the epoch and ties it to the producer id. Every write and every commit carries that epoch, and the broker checks it.

The sequence is what makes this robust. Producer A initializes and gets, say, epoch five, then a partition isolates it mid-transaction. The orchestrator starts a fresh producer B with the same transactional id, B initializes, the coordinator bumps the epoch to six and aborts A's in-flight transaction, and B becomes the one true owner. When the partition heals and the zombie A tries to commit at its old epoch five, the broker compares five against the current six and rejects it with a ProducerFenced error. That error is fatal by design, so A closes itself and its stale writes and commit never become visible.

On the National Bank of India settlement service this is exactly how we stop a double credit. If the settlement pod that was crediting Priya loses the network and a replacement takes over, the replacement bumps the epoch, so when the old pod reconnects and tries to finish the same transfer, its commit is fenced and Priya is credited exactly once. Consumers reading with read-committed isolation never see the zombie's uncommitted records, because there is no valid commit marker for them.

The nuances I always mention are these. Idempotence, which transactions require, deduplicates ordinary producer retries within one session using the producer id, epoch, and per-partition sequence numbers, while the epoch bump is what fences an entire second instance. Each logical producer role needs its own stable transactional id, because two real producers sharing one id would fence each other endlessly. And Kafka's fencing only protects writes inside Kafka; if the same operation also touches a database, I use the transactional outbox pattern, because epoch fencing will not roll back a database write. Understanding epoch fencing is really understanding how Kafka keeps exactly-once correct even when the network lies to you about who is alive.
